text: I’ll treat the requested 1100 mm tread length as the exposed radial span from the 100 mm-radius column to the 1200 mm-radius shaft wall. Each tread is a 250 mm-wide horizontal rectangular slab; it extends into the column solid and slightly through the shaft wall before subtraction so the final air volume has watertight column/tread/wall junctions. Tread tops are at 150, 300, …, 3000 mm, with 18° rotation increments. I’ll first construct the exact fluid volume in metres and inspect a coarse tessellation.

The coarse view shows one connected air volume and the intended two-turn spiral. I’ll now inspect the resulting boundary faces by analytic surface type and elevation so the five requested patch names are assigned to the actual post-boolean faces, including all tread/column/wall junction splits.

The inspection caught a construction issue before meshing: build123d’s default cylinder is centred about z=0, so it clipped away the upper half of the stair. I’ll correct the enclosure to span z=0…3 m and use explicit alignment for every tread (axis-to-wall in x, centred in y, bottom-aligned in z), then remeasure and redraw.

The corrected coarse model contains all 20 treads, with horizontal obstacle faces at each bottom/top elevation; the last tread top coincides with the 3 m opening plane, so only its surrounding free area belongs to the opening. I’ll assign the two analytic cylindrical faces by their known radii, the z=0 and z=3 planar faces as floor/opening, and all remaining post-boolean planar faces as tread surfaces, then export all five patches in one conformal tessellation.

The exporter’s installed API uses `out_dir` rather than `output_dir`; no geometry operation failed. I’ll repeat the face assignment in a self-contained accepted cell and export with the correct argument.
I’ll make the export cell reproducible by importing `export_patches` within the accepted cell, while retaining the same conformal patch assignment.

The exported union is watertight and conformal (7,198 triangles, zero open/non-manifold/flipped edges). I’ll use `snappyHexMesh` with an enclosing Cartesian background mesh and retain the point `(0.5, 0, 0.05)` m, safely inside the air below the first tread. A 0.10 m base cell with two surface refinement levels gives about 0.025 m near the 0.04 m tread thickness.
The background mesh is 21,632 cells at exactly 0.10 m. I’ll now cut and snap it to the five-patch closed surface with 0.025 m near-surface cells.
OpenFOAM 2512 requires minimal `fvSchemes` and `fvSolution` dictionaries even for this mesh-only case. I’ll add empty valid dictionaries and rerun the unchanged mesher.
The mesher parsed all five STL files but requires an explicit empty `features` list when feature snapping is disabled. I’ll add that required entry and rerun.
The snapped mesh completed with 206,748 cells and no mesher quality errors. I’ll run the binding `checkMesh` and inspect patch sizes and enclosed volume before finalizing.

`checkMesh` passes: one region, five boundary patches, 206,748 cells, 13.2445 m³, maximum non-orthogonality 52.6°, and maximum skewness 1.51. The mesh volume differs from the exact CAD air volume by about 0.044%, consistent with surface snapping. I’ll make one final colored boundary rendering to visually verify patch placement.
The OpenFOAM reader groups individual patches under a nested `boundary` block. I’ll render from that block directly and print each mesh patch’s face count.

The final rendering confirms the five patches are correctly placed and individually present. All requested dimensions were measured from the constructed geometry; no requested geometric property remains unchecked. The only modeling assumptions are that tread 1 has its top at 150 mm, tread 20 has its top flush with the 3000 mm opening, and “250 mm deep” is a rectangular tangential width.
